transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-02-14
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Jon (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood SRE), Daniel (Equinox Head ML), Priya (Infra), Marco (ML Eng)
Shared artifacts: Redwood KV deep-dive deck (link), benchmark traces (https://redwood.app/benchmarks/equinox-kv-trace-2026-02-14), S3 log snippet (s3://equinox-logs/kv/trace-0214)

Summary:
- Deep dive into KV cache eviction patterns customers are seeing; focus on long-context sessions, prefix reuse, and paging to NVMe.
- Discussed tuning knobs: slice size, per-shard capacity, eviction policy (LRU vs LFU), eager warming, and prefix-aware caching.
- Agreed next steps: reproduce with customer's traces, share eviction heatmaps, plan sizing for Private/VPC deployment.

Topics:
- KV cache eviction and root causes (memory vs shard imbalance)
- Paging strategies and NVMe-backed spill behavior
- Long-context handling and prefix reuse semantics
- Interaction with batching and quantization on latency/throughput
- Security/residency considerations for Private deployments (KMS, audit logs)

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Ava: All right everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna try to get through the KV cache architecture and the eviction behaviour you saw last week, uh, and figure out next steps. I'm gonna hand over to Jon for the deep tech part.
[00:16] Jon: Cool, thanks Ava. Hey Daniel, Priya, Marco - quick context, we pulled the traces you sent and some of the patterns look like heavy long-context sessions with a lot of prefix reuse, which interacts oddly with shard-level eviction. I'll share my screen in a sec.
[00:32] Daniel: Yep, thanks. To restate, we saw intermittent latency spikes and some failures where latency jumped and then tokens were re-requested which caused throughput drops. We suspected kv-cache evictions but not sure why it kicked in.
[00:44] Jon: Right, so two vectors to look at: first is memory pressure inside the GPU addressable KV cache; second is the logical eviction policy and shard hotness. In our runtime each model host maintains per-shard KV capacity and we do LRU-ish eviction, but under high prefix reuse LRU can evict needed entries because reuse isn't uniformly recent across shards.
[01:10] Marco: Quick q, by "per-shard" do you mean per-GPU shard or per-model-slice? We have multi-seq workloads and sometimes requests get routed across pods.
[01:22] Jon: Good question. In Redwood Serving we shard the KV cache across GPUs - like 8 shards for an 8-GPU host. Each shard has a capacity (configured in tokens/bytes). Requests that map to a token key land on the owning shard. If your prefix reuse is concentrated on one shard, that shard goes hot and evicts more aggressively.
[01:38] Priya: That fits our observation - one node's NPU (we use A100s) showed high mem pressure; others idle-ish. Is there auto-rebalancing?
[01:48] Maya: There's no live rebalancing of hot keys between shards today; we rely on routing and fallback to other replicas. For Dedicated/Private you can size shards or increase replication. Also can enable prefix-aware routing to try to keep prefixes co-located but that has tradeoffs.
[02:05] Daniel: Prefix-aware routing sounds promising - how does that work?
[02:10] Jon: It's basically sticky routing for known high-reuse prefixes: we maintain a small prefix index that maps frequent prefixes to a preferred host. New incoming requests with that prefix go to that host to maximize cache hits. But if the host is overloaded we still have fallbacks. Note: index syncing adds small control-plane overhead.
[02:28] Priya: Any risk of hot-spotting and OSS implications?
[02:32] Jon: Yep, if you route everything to a single host you can create hot spots. So we combine prefix routing with weighted balancing - and in Private you can specify reserve replicas for heavy prefixes.
[02:44] Marco: About eviction policy - you said LRU-ish; can we use LFU or TTLs?
[02:49] Jon: We support TTLs and an adaptive LFU hybrid in beta. For long-running prefixes LFU often helps because frequently used tokens stay; LRU will evict if they aren't recently used. The config knobs: per-shard capacity, min-resident for prefix tokens, eviction policy.
[03:05] Daniel: The logs we saw had sudden page-out to NVMe - is that paging to disk part of the runtime?
[03:12] Jon: By default we don't page to disk for production Hosted; but for Dedicated/Private customers with large contexts we have NVMe-backed paging where cold KV pages spill to local SSD. That reduces GPU memory pressure but adds tail latency when pages are faulted back.
[03:30] Priya: Our ops team saw io stalls during faults; are there prefetching options?
[03:35] Maya: Yes, we have predictive prefetching based on access patterns. For predictable prefix sequences we can pre-warm the NVMe->GPU path. Prefetch reduces tail but can increase IO and read amplification. It's a tradeoff.
[03:50] Marco: How much tail latency are we talking about on an NVMe fault?
[03:54] Jon: It depends on the SSD and PCIe gen. On our CI hardware a cold fault can add 20-50 ms; on consumer NVMe it was 40-120 ms. These are worst-case. So if your SLO is tight (e.g., 100 ms) paging can violate it.
[04:11] Daniel: We did see spikes around that in the logs, matching user sessions that were long and had cold prefixes.
[04:17] Priya: Is there a way to see per-prefix cache hit rates and eviction counters?
[04:22] Jon: Yes - the Console exposes per-route and per-prefix metrics in the tracing UI; but for your Dedicated test we can surface a higher fidelity heatmap and per-shard eviction timeline. That's one of the artifacts we'll share.
[04:35] Ava: (interrupt) we'll attach the eviction heatmap as a CSV and the trace. Jon, you said earlier about shard sizing - can you walk through sizing heuristics?
[04:45] Jon: Sure. Heuristics: 1) compute token distribution percentiles - 95th token length and prefix reuse frequency; 2) estimate unique tokens resident for high-reuse prefixes; 3) allocate per-shard capacity with headroom for burst factor (1.5-2x). If you have long contexts the effective resident tokens per session multiply. For multi-tenancy we also reserve per-tenant minima.
[05:11] Marco: Does quantization affect KV sizes? We are running 4-bit quantized weights - how does that interplay?
[05:17] Jon: Good point. Quantization reduces model weight memory, but KV cache entries are stored as key/value pairs (attention keys/values) usually in FP16 or FP32 depending on runtime. We have quantization-friendly storage for values that can compress to FP16 or custom 8-bit in some setups. The impact: lower model memory can free GPU capacity for larger KV caches, but precision tradeoffs may affect model quality on long contexts.
[05:40] Daniel: So if we enable 8-bit KV compression, we might see different quality?
[05:44] Jon: Potentially. We recommend testing on a prompt set. Redwood Optimize surfaced that for some generative workloads 8-bit KV compression had negligible impact; for summarization you might see regressions. We'll include a small eval run.
[05:58] Priya: About long-context, do you split prefixes? We have sessions that append a conversation history of 30k tokens.
[06:05] Jon: Two approaches: 1) KV paging+spill so you keep full context but pay I/O when re-faulting; 2) prefix/windowing - chunk conversation into overlapping windows and reuse prefix keys across windows. Prefix reuse means keys from the front are still referenced; if windows are overlapped well you can reduce misses. The tradeoff is more compute when you re-encode prefixes.
[06:26] Marco: Any heuristics for overlap size?
[06:29] Jon: Overlap typically 50-100 tokens for chat is common; for tasks needing longer coherence 512-1024 might be needed. Also prefix-aware caching reduces duplication.
[06:39] Priya: We saw weird evictions where a reused prefix was evicted and re-decoded, causing extra latency and token duplication - is that consistent with your hot-shard behaviour?
[06:47] Jon: Yep. If a shard evicts a key, the next request must re-attend and regenerate KV entries, which adds compute and can result in double work. If requests arrive concurrently and both miss, you get duplicate work unless the runtime deduplicates inflight recomputes. We do have an inflight dedupe mechanism but it has edge cases.
[07:06] Maya: Also worth mentioning that caching at the application level (prefix caching) can reduce this. You can materialize frequently used prefixes and attach them as context, so runtime doesn't have to re-derive them.
[07:18] Daniel: We tried app-level prefix caching but our tokenization boundaries mismatch sometimes, and we saw slightly different tokens due to whitespace differences etc. Any guidance?
[07:27] Jon: Normalization is key - ensure you canonicalize whitespace and punctuation, use the same tokenizer version, and ideally hash the exact token sequence. We can provide a small canonicalizer util.
[07:38] Marco: Regarding routing: you mentioned fallback to replicas. How fast is fallback and does it double requests?
[07:44] Jon: Fallback is synchronous with a small exponential backoff. It shouldn't double requests in steady state, but during failover window you can see duplicates. We also support async fallbacks where the primary serves and replicas sync in background.
[07:58] Priya: For our Private deployment we're concerned about KMS overhead when paging keys encrypted to disk. Is encryption impacting perf?
[08:06] Maya: Encrypting pages at-rest with KMS adds crypto overhead on page-out and page-in. We use local HSM-friendly caches so typical CPU overhead is modest but can add ~1-3 ms per page op. Also network KMS calls should be minimized by using cached DEKs (data encryption keys) locally. We'll include recommended KMS patterns.
[08:26] Daniel: Good. Our compliance team will want the audit trail for page-in/page-out events. Can Redwood log those?
[08:31] Ava: Yes, Private includes audit logs for KV operations at a coarse granularity; we can enable finer logs by request but that increases storage. We'll share the audit doc.
[08:41] Marco: Back to eviction - what is best practice for policy selection?
[08:45] Jon: If your workload has hot prefixes that are frequently reused over time, LFU-hybrid works best. If temporal locality dominates (recent tokens matter more) LRU is fine. TTLs are useful for ephemeral sessions. Also ensure per-shard capacity and headroom are sized correctly.
[08:59] Priya: How do we measure hotness? We can compute top-k token prefixes from traces?
[09:04] Jon: Exactly - compute prefix frequencies and map them to shards. We'll help run an analysis over your traces. The heatmap will show shards and top prefixes.
[09:16] Daniel: Can you explain prefix reuse vs prefix collision? We suspect different users share similar prefixes and cause eviction noise.
[09:23] Jon: Prefix collision is when distinct logical prefixes hash to same keys - in our system keys are derived from token sequences, so collisions are rare. What you likely see is multi-tenant interference: different users' prefixes that are large and frequently used occupy the same shard capacity, causing eviction of one another. Tenant isolation (reserved minima) can help.
[09:45] Marco: What about batching interaction? If we batch many requests cloth-peak around same time, does that change eviction profile?
[09:52] Jon: Batching improves throughput but can increase concurrency to the same shard which temporarily raises memory pressure. The runtime does queueing and streaming; optimizing batch sizes and concurrency per host reduces pressure. We recommend smaller, more frequent batches for low-latency workloads to avoid large concurrent KV spikes.
[10:10] Priya: Any tooling to simulate our request mix?
[10:13] Jon: Yes we have a load generator script that replays traces with timing and token lengths. We'll run it against a staging cluster with your params.
[10:21] Daniel: You mentioned inflight dedupe earlier - are there cases where it fails?
[10:25] Jon: It can fail if requests miss and are routed to different replicas before the dedupe token index syncs. For strongly consistent dedupe you need single-writer routing or shared dedupe metadata. We're working on cross-host dedupe but it's not GA.
[10:41] Marco: Could we workaround by routing high-reuse prefixes to single host?
[10:45] Jon: Yes, that's the prefix-sticky model - but accept the hotspot tradeoff. Alternatively, use replication for heavily used prefixes.
[10:53] Priya: Regarding paging thresholds, what is the default trigger for spilling to NVMe?
[10:57] Jon: We spill when GPU resident KV bytes exceed configured per-shard bytes. Default is conservative; for Dedicated we recommend raising it and relying on NVMe for extreme tails.
[11:08] Daniel: Is there a way to do soft-eviction before spilling?
[11:12] Jon: Soft-evict marks entries as candidate for removal and permits immediate rehydration with no disk op for a short grace period kept in CPU memory. That reduces immediate fault cost but adds RAM overhead.
[11:24] Marco: Are there metrics for soft-evict hits vs hard-evict faults?
[11:28] Jon: Yes - Console exposes soft eviction hits, hard faults, and cold-fault latencies. We'll make sure those panels are in your dashboard.
[11:37] Priya: For on-prem we might want to disable paging and just scale GPUs - what are tradeoffs?
[11:43] Maya: More GPUs increases cost but avoids IO tail. If you can dedicate enough GPU headroom you get best latency predictability. Paging helps cost tradeoffs by letting you serve larger contexts with fewer GPUs but with tail risk.
[11:58] Daniel: Any quick wins we can do now to reduce our incidents?
[12:01] Jon: Short term: 1) canonicalize prefixes at app layer, 2) enable per-tenant minima for heavy tenants, 3) tune batch sizing to reduce concurrent spikes, 4) enable soft-evict if you want to avoid immediate faults. We'll include config snippets.
[12:18] Priya: Let's talk SLOs - if we expect p95 under 200ms, what should we do?
[12:23] Jon: For p95 200ms, avoid NVMe paging on common path. Either scale GPU capacity to avoid spills or ensure predictive prefetch warms common prefixes. Also set batch sizes conservatively. We'll run a p95 simulation.
[12:36] Daniel: One of our concerns: when a prefix is re-decoded we sometimes see token mismatches and duplication downstream - is that due to race on KV updates?
[12:44] Jon: Could be. If two replicas recompute and one writes back slightly different past tokens due to subtleties (tokenizer differences or decoding nondeterminism) you can see divergence. Use canonical tokenizer and deterministic decoding for prefix materialization.
[12:58] Marco: Are there recommended tokenizer/hash functions we should use?
[13:02] Jon: Use the same model tokenizer binary and an exact token sequence hash (sha256 of token ids). We'll provide a small util that generates canonical keys.
[13:12] Priya: On the network side, we run in a VPC with strict egress rules. Any special setup for Private?
[13:18] Ava: For Private we ship a control-plane agent that runs in your VPC and communicates over private endpoints. No egress needed for model traffic; S3/KMS calls can be routed via VPC endpoints. We'll provide a deployment checklist.
[13:31] Daniel: If we move to Private, will the set of KV features change? For example, will NVMe paging be supported?
[13:38] Jon: Private supports the same runtime features; you manage the NVMe and we provide the config. Some features like cross-host dedupe might require control-plane linkage which can be optional.
[13:49] Marco: About observability - will we get flamegraphs of where time is spent (recompute vs page-in vs model forward)?
[13:56] Jon: Yes. We surface per-token timing breakdowns: KV hit, page-fault, recompute forward pass time. We'll add a per-route flamegraph.
[14:06] Priya: Can you share the exact config snippet for soft-evict and prefix-reservation?
[14:11] Jon: I'll paste in the meeting notes doc; high level: 
- cache.eviction.policy: "adaptive_lfu"
- cache.shard_capacity_bytes: "<computed>"
- cache.soft_evict_enabled: true
- cache.prefix_reservation: {"<prefix_hash>": "min_resident_tokens"}  (we'll give exact syntax in doc)
[14:34] Ava: Ok we're at about 45 minutes in; want to cover any remaining questions and then recap next steps.
[14:41] Daniel: One final — are there any known bugs that could explain sudden complete flushes? We saw a full host-level flush once.
[14:48] Maya: Full flushes usually happen during node restart/OOM or explicit admin flush. There was a bug in an earlier runtime that could double-free cache metadata on rare races — that's fixed in 2026.1. We'll check your runtime version.
[15:02] Marco: How do we verify our runtime version?
[15:05] Jon: We log it at startup; you can query /health or the console. We'll also run a quick version check in the repro run.
[15:12] Daniel: Great. Thanks everyone.

Recap:
- Redwood to reproduce eviction with traces, produce eviction heatmap and per-shard timelines.

Artifacts to send: eviction heatmap CSV, benchmark replay script, config snippets, security/compliance checklist, benchmark spreadsheet (latency vs cost).
